entries.title: Chicago Archdiocese settles 9 sex abuse claims for $5.4 million
entries.summary: <p>The Archdiocese of Chicago recently settled out of court with nine people who accused eight Chicago-area priests of sexually abusing them decades ago. </p><p>The settlements, totaling $5.4 million, were all reached in the last two weeks, according to the attorneys representing the victims. </p><p>"Nobody's paying that kind of money for something that didn't happen," said Marc Pearlman, one of the victim's attorneys, during a Thursday news conference announcing the settlements. "This is validation that it happened." </p><p>The allegations date as far back as the early 1970s and as recently as the late 1990s. The victims' ages at the time of the abuse ranged from 6 to 14 years old.</p><p>The list of accused priests, most of whom have died, and their Chicago-area parishes are: </p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: In CBP officer's rape trial, woman describes alleged attack at Schaumburg hotel: 'He showed a badge'
entries.summary: <p>A New York woman<b> </b>sobbed<b> </b>at the end of a lengthy day on the witness stand Thursday, after she insisted she’d been “robbed and raped”<b> </b>by a man rumored to be a “fake cop”<b> </b>during a visit to Chicago’s northwest suburbs<b> </b>in 2022.</p><p>She testified during the trial of U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer<b> </b>Luis Uribe, 45. Not only did Uribe work a real job in law enforcement, federal prosecutors say he used his gun and badge to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" >sexually assault four women</a><b> </b>in Schaumburg and Naperville.</p><p>But confusion abounded when Uribe’s defense attorney tried to sort through the details of the woman’s visit to the suburb of Schaumburg. The woman is a native of China who became a U.S. citizen in 2003. She speaks little English, so she testified with help from a translator.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" >Border Protection officer accused of sex assaults became ‘perfect mark’ for prostitution ring, lawyer says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>She struggled when it came time to identify Uribe in the courtroom. She told Uribe’s attorney he had things “all messed up”<b> </b>as he tried to identify associates she referred to as “pretty girl,” “beauty”<b> </b>or<b> </b>“sister.”</p><p>However, the woman gave a clear answer when a prosecutor asked what happened to her.</p><p>“He robbed me of my money,” she said. “He raped me.”</p><p>The feds say Uribe committed<b> </b>six attacks<b> </b>between February and October 2022, but his attorney told jurors Wednesday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" target="_blank" >he’d been set up</a> by a prostitution ring overseen by a boss in China. He admitted Uribe visited prostitutes and is a “flawed”<b> </b>human being, but he said there’s no proof that Uribe robbed and raped the women, as prosecutors allege.</p><p>The 67-year-old woman who testified Thursday told jurors she came to Chicago in October 2022 because a friend of hers wanted her “to check out some casinos here.”<b> </b>She said she referred to the friend as “beauty,”<b> </b>and she brought along $3,000.</p><p>She also acknowledged she’d seen a photo of Uribe on the social messaging app WeChat, and she was told he was a “fake cop.”</p><p>The photo was taken during a meeting at a seafood buffet in Hoffman Estates, according to the feds.</p><p>The woman was attacked while staying in a Schaumburg<b> </b>Days Inn, jurors heard. The woman explained Thursday how she heard a knock on her hotel room door and opened it, thinking it was a member of the hotel staff.</p><p>That’s when a man rushed in, she said, wearing a hat, a black jacket and pants.</p><p>“Immediately he closed the door and he showed a badge,”<b> </b>the woman testified.</p><p>He pushed a chair against the door, put the badge and a gun on a table, and asked for cash, she said. The woman told jurors she gave him “all my money.”</p><p>“I was terrified,” she said. “He had a gun.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" >O’Hare-based Border Protection officer sexually abused, robbed women at gunpoint, indictment claims</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>She said he forced her to take off her clothes and perform oral sex. Then, she said, he pulled her to the bed<b> </b>and raped her. When it was over, she said he pushed her into the shower area,<b> </b>put his clothing back on and escaped.</p><p>The woman said she tried to tell the hotel staff she’d been robbed, but she struggled because of her difficulty with English. So she went to a woman she’d met earlier at the hotel — who also happened to be Chinese. </p><p>Early in her testimony, prosecutors asked the alleged victim to identify Uribe in the courtroom. She initially failed to do so and eventually broke down crying, prompting a break in the proceedings. But later, while describing the attack, she pointed and told the translator she’d seen someone who “might be that person.”</p><p>During his cross-examination, defense attorney Michael Clancy<b> </b>asked the woman whether a “boss believed that you were coming to Chicago to work for her and [to] be a sex worker?” The woman said she “didn’t agree”<b> </b>to that arrangement.</p><p>“At my old age, I only agreed to come here to check it out to play,” the woman said, referring to the casinos.</p><p>Still, she admitted learning<b> </b>the second Chinese woman at the hotel was a sex worker.</p><p>Before testimony wrapped for the day, jurors heard the initial testimony of that second woman, who is 54 and also lives in New York. She acknowledged for prosecutors that she did massage work with “a sexual component”<b> </b>and had a “boss”<b> </b>who found her clients.</p><p>She said her boss sent her to the Chicago area<b> </b>in 2022 and showed her the photo of Uribe at the seafood buffet. Then, during her stay at the Schaumburg Days Inn, she said she encountered the first woman “in a terrible state, ready to cry”<b> </b>— and pointing to a photo.</p><p>The woman allegedly told her, “the fake police robbed her and raped her.”</p>
entries.author: Jon Seidel

entries.title: Hagen Smith's multi-inning relief assignment could be the recipe for other White Sox starter prospects
entries.summary: <p>Former fifth overall pick <b>Hagen Smith</b> made his first career major league start on Thursday night.</p><p>But his two scoreless innings before giving way to <b>Erick Fedde</b> represents an extension of the White Sox’ league-leading usage of openers, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/24/white-sox-hagen-smith-brian-bannister-will-venable-2024-draft-jac-caglianone-konnor-griffin-trey-yesavage-pitching-development-pete-crow-armstrong" target="_blank" ><u>not a deviation from Smith’s conversion to relief</u></a> for the rest of the season.</p><p>That Smith’s first two full years in pro ball have been defined by a sluggish, physically challenging first halves before a strong finishing kick, is part of why he’s in the bullpen.</p><p>“The last couple of years, the first half of the season has been marred a little bit by an injury -- nothing serious–but in the second half of both last year and what it looks like this year, he’s come back after the injury and been really good,” said Sox farm director <b>Paul Janish</b>.</p><p>With a 0.50 ERA and 26 strikeouts in 18 innings, Smith’s adjustment is going swimmingly, though the 10 walks lend a reliever flavor to his work. With 16 games left, Smith’s role could be the sort of opportunity Triple-A starters <b>Jonathan Cannon, Noah Schultz, Drew Thorpe </b>or <b>David Sandlin </b>should anticipate.</p><p>“It’s very reasonable, as we’ve seen, that they would pitch in a bulk role,” Janish said. “Potentially start as well. But the bulk option is definitely something that they’re aware of and they’re ready for.”</p><p>The most immediate candidate would be Sandlin, who has a 1.90 ERA and 31.7% strikeout rate in four starts since he was last optioned, and is rested after not making his originally scheduled Thursday outing for the Knights.</p><p>“Sandlin’s been locked in,” Janish said. “The integrity of the stuff’s been really good. Feel comfortable saying he’s probably in as confident of a place that he’s been in a little while.”</p><p>Opening day starter <b>Shane Smith </b>is working in single-inning relief in Triple-A for now, but Janish anticipates him competing for a rotation spot next spring.</p><h3><b>Nearly no-hit</b></h3><p>Already limited to five runs in their first two losses to a Pirates team playing out the string, the Sox offense–<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/09/white-sox-hitting-director-ryan-fuller-talks-offensive-improvement-and-the-development-that-remains-colson-montgomery-munetaka-murakami-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" ><u>still their best unit in years</u></a>–did not register a hit off hard-throwing 25-year-old right-hander <b>Jared Jones </b>in Thursday night’s series finale until <b>Colson Montgomery’s </b>two-out double off the wall in seventh.</p><p>In keeping with the theme of the week, the runner was stranded by a <b>Braden Montgomery </b>lineout.</p><h3><b>Antonacci’s identity</b></h3><p><b>Tristan Peters </b>wearing a t-shirt with a picture of <b>Sam Antonacci</b> made to look like a mugshot the day after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/09/white-sox-pushing-back-luis-castillo-for-mechanical-work-as-rotation-stays-in-flux-sean-burke-davis-martin-david-sandlin-noah-schultz-drew-thorpe-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>his dustup with Pirates second baseman </u><b><u>Brandon Lowe</u></b></a> might be a coincidence, but is in line with how the team feels about their inflammatory rookie.</p><p>“I don’t think he spends a whole lot of time worrying about making friends,” said Janish. “He has an edge to him. He plays the game hard. I don’t care what era you’re playing in, he was going to be good at this game.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Tristan Peters’ disembodied torso is draped in a show of solidarity with Sam Antonacci <a href="https://t.co/ifUteIsQSa">pic.twitter.com/ifUteIsQSa</a></p>— James Fegan (@JRFegan) <a href="https://x.com/JRFegan/status/2098161260873318484?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p></p><h3><b>Steak and eggs</b></h3><p>Power-hitting prospect <b>Caleb Bonemer </b>will play largely, if not exclusively in the outfield during the Arizona Fall League this October. The position is more demanding on his legs than the infield, but even after 36 home runs, the 20-year-old Bonemer feels fresher than he did at this point last season.</p><p>It’s a credit to his diet and the strength he added in the winter.</p><p>“I was pretty much eating as much steak and eggs as I possibly could,” Bonemer told the Sun-Times.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Memories of 9/11 horror still fresh after a quarter-century
entries.summary: <p>On Sept. 11, 2001, my older son was 5, and some mornings played video games on my computer. So I wasn't plugged into the world that morning. I didn't know that American Airlines Flight 11 had struck the North Tower at 7:46 a.m. Chicago time. I did not own a cell phone.</p><p>At the Northbrook Metra station, stepping onto the 8:17 Downtown, I heard a woman down the platform say something about the World Trade Center being hit by a plane.</p><p>At Union Station, knots of people stood around, talking. I asked one: what kind of plane hit the twin towers?</p><p>"A 767," he said. That startled me. I had assumed it would be a Cessna.</p><p>"That's a big plane," I said, thickly.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-cd0000" name="module-cd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>At Wacker Drive, people were pouring out of the Sears Tower, fanning out in all directions. I noticed that, as they hurried along, they looked up, scanning the sky. As if they expected to see a plane go into the building at any moment.</p><p>There was a Billy Goat Tavern on Washington, open for breakfast. I stepped inside. Everyone was just standing there in silence, watching the North Tower collapse on TV. I joined them. You could hear the eggs sizzling on the grill.</p><p>The paper was still at 401 N. Wabash. I was on the editorial board and walked into editorial page editor Steve Huntley's office.</p><p>"How do you spell 'Osama bin Laden?'" he asked. I'd never heard the name but went to my office to find out.</p><p>I used to say there were two shocks about Sept. 11 — the first was that it happened, that four planes were hijacked by 19 men wielding box cutters. Two crashed into New York's World Trade Center, toppling the towers. A third hit the Pentagon and a fourth crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers stormed the cockpit; 2,973 men, women and children died that day.</p><p>There was a time when I wouldn't feel obligated to spell out the details. But more than a third of Americans have no living memory of Sept. 11, 2001, and it would not be surprising if 9/11 is news to some — just another crumb of dusty history they didn't learn in school.</p><p>Leading to the second shock of 9/11: that it went away, or at least ebbed. Because for days and weeks and months, it seemed that 9/11 was a permanent condition, a radiating, bottomless shock, sorrow and stupefaction. But ebb it did, slowly receding, like a tide going out. And now 25 years have gone by, and attention must be paid again.</p><p>We put out "Extras" in those days — special editions to update breaking news stories, hawked at newsstands downtown. Our first was headlined "UNSPEAKABLE HORROR" — I remember looking at "Unspeakable" and thinking, "Really? 'Cause we're trying to flippin' speak it." The second was better: "TERROR!" </p><p>I filed an insert to our editorial, then asked the City Desk what I could do to help. Go into the Loop, see what's up. So I went back to the Sears Tower and interviewed disappointed tourists who had planned to visit the Sky Deck. At 111 W. Washington, I watched an employee, ex-Marine Johnny Washington, lower the building's flags to half-mast.</p><p>"This is terrible," he said. </p><p>Back at the newsroom, John Cruickshank, a smart and decent Canadian who was co-editor of the paper, made a little speech. This was the biggest story of our lives, yes, but it is also an enormous human tragedy. We should pray. So we all bowed our head and uttered a little silent prayer, then went back to work. I'm not generally a fan of public displays of piety, but it seemed the right thing to do, and I was grateful.</p><p>I won't attempt to summarize all the bad that came from those attacks. Two needless wars, in Afghanistan and Iraq. Over 7,000 U.S. military deaths — twice the loss of 9/11 — not to forget over 200,000 civilian deaths. I don't recall that being called a genocide. The sweeping, intrusive Patriot Act. George W. Bush tried not to demonize Muslims, but others were not so scrupulous — anti-Islamic hate was a major leg of Donald Trump's winning campaigns, and he barred immigration wholesale from Muslim countries. </p><p>On Sept. 12, 2001, I showed my older boy the front page of the New York Times, its photo of an explosion boiling out of the World Trade Center, and asked him what he thought about the picture, worried how he was processing 9/11's enormity. He said it looked beautiful — he thought it was a flower, a red rose, and I didn't correct him. The horror was very hard to wrap your mind around. It still is.</p>

entries.title: Slowed by injury, White Sox catcher Kyle Teel still has tools for a breakout
entries.summary: <p>Back in June, Kyle Teel’s first home run of the season, was preceded by a talking to in the dugout from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> manager Will Venable.</p><p>The gist: Go easier on yourself. It’ll come.</p><p>Instead, Teel ended up missing another six weeks with an injury, and now he’s likely to finish with fewer than 40-regular season games in his second season in the majors.</p><p>As the Sox guard a slim lead in the American League Central standings, the stakes of every at-bat have risen, and the temptation to press is there for the 24-year-old tapped to be their long-term solution behind the plate.</p><p>Reminded of his conversation with Venable about going easier on himself, Teel conceded, “It’s a great point.”</p><p>“Not trying to do everything at once, not trying to figure everything out at once, is important, while still having the urgency to get to where you want to be,” he told the Sun-Times on Thursday. “My biggest thing is, how can I do a job and put us in the best situation?”</p><p>Teel said his pitch-framing — a huge part of why the Sox regard his defense so highly — is slightly better from last season, going by a small sample. On offense, the two home runs he has popped in five games since returning from his sprained left ankle have lent a glow to his production, but he’s still hitting .195/.271/.377 on the season.</p><p>After the work he did to bulk up and add strength over the winter, that’s not the breakout the Sox had anticipated in the spring.</p><p>“He has bigger movements to get the slack out of his swing,” hitting director Ryan Fuller said. “He has done an amazing job of being stronger, more stable, where those movements just get a little bit more refined and tighter. So it’s not going to be as big of a move to get his swing off.”</p><p>It’s less than 100 plate appearances, but Statcast data shows that Teel is yet <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/09/white-sox-hitting-director-ryan-fuller-talks-offensive-improvement-and-the-development-that-remains-colson-montgomery-munetaka-murakami-miguel-vargas-chase-meidroth" target="_blank" ><u>another White Sox hitter who has seen a significant jump (3 mph) in bat speed</u></a>. Pulling the ball in the air for power more was his explicit goal last season, and the same data shows he’s catching pitches out in front more than his rookie year, where he hit an impressive .273/.375/.411 but also lifted a mild eight homers in 78 games.</p><p>Perhaps the most encouraging element for Teel is that on the heels of blasting a 96 mph fastball out of the park to right field Tuesday night, his swing feels the same as it always has.</p><p>“The thing is, I’m not trying to pull it in the air, either — I’m just trying to put a good swing on the ball,” he said. “I would love to tell you that I made a huge adjustment, or something feels different than last year. But honestly, swinging the bat, I feel like it all just comes down to getting my at-bats, and that’s something I’m lacking this year, just being hurt. The more at-bats I get, the more settled in I feel.”</p><p>When the Sox fly to St. Louis for this weekend’s series with the Cardinals, they’ll have just 16 games left in their schedule, not much time for settling in.</p><p>“I would just say I focus on my process every single day,” Teel said. “The results aren’t always going to come, but if I can refine my process and accomplish what I want every single at-bat, that’s all I can do. That’s all anyone can do, really.”</p><p>He noted that he needs to downgrade the goal of “accomplish what I want” to more granular goals, such as moving a runner over, swinging at the right pitch or making the opposing pitcher work — not just hitting an 112 mph home run every time.</p><p>But what’s clear even after three separate leg injuries in 2026 is that the Sox are prepared to be patient with Teel long-term — trusting that it’ll come.</p><p>“He’s a guy back there,” Venable said. “We plan on being there as our starting catcher.”</p>

entries.title: Man critically wounded in Humboldt Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was critically injured in a shooting in Humboldt Park Thursday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, whose age wasn’t known, was in the 800 block of North Kedzie Avenue at 5:09 p.m. when he was approached by someone and shot in the face and head, police said. </p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Maine South beats New Trier in Big Ten-bound quarterback showdown
entries.summary: <p>The most anticipated New Trier vs. Maine South matchup in a decade contained all the ingredients for a special night.</p><p>Trevians’ quarterback Jackie Ryder is a Purdue recruit and a late-blooming local star. Jameson Purcell, the Maine South quarterback, has been in the spotlight for three years and is heading to Indiana.</p><p>New Trier opened the season with three wins and arrived in the Super 25 just in time for the showdown with the Hawks.</p><p>Both quarterbacks played well, and the scoring went back and forth until Keaton Vitel’s 98-yard kickoff return touchdown provided the little extra magic <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/06/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >No. 13 Maine South</a> needed to pull away with a 35-28 win against the No. 24 Trevians on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/10/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Thursday</a> in Northfield.</p><p>“We were going crazy,” Purcell said. “That is exactly what we needed. [New Trier] scored and then [Vitel] took it to the house. He really just took the air out of them. It was a crucial play. They had momentum, and we took it right from them.”</p><p>Vitel caught an 18-yard touchdown pass from Purcell in the first quarter and was an impact player in the defensive secondary as well.</p><p>Ryder scored on a four-yard run to cut Maine South’s lead to 21-14 midway through the third quarter. But the home crowd barely had a chance to celebrate before Vitel scored.</p><p>“We knew we had to bring some energy,” Vitel said. “They told me to take it up our sideline. All I was thinking was, I’m going to wait and be patient until I see the hole and then I’m going to hit the hole. I saw the hole, and it was just the kicker, and I broke it, and I knew I wasn’t going to go down.”</p><p>New Trier (3-1, 0-1 CSL South) battled back to cut the deficit to 28-21 on a trick-play touchdown pass from Ryder to running back Throy Nightengale Jr. to receiver John Baxter.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2e0000" name="image-2e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4073f87/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/381b1a9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5a6058/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="New Trier's Jackie Ryder (5) looks for a receiver during the game against Maine South. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5a6058/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4824cc0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5a6058/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3159x1773+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff7%2Fb1%2F3daddf8a475481d7ab7a14a85379%2Fob-cst-091126-010-1.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>New Trier’s Jackie Ryder (5) looks for a receiver during the game against Maine South.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Kirsten Stickney/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Maine South (3-1, 1-0) leaned on its offensive line and tough runs from Payton Donaldson, Matt Schlenhardt and Purcell to eat up the clock and keep the ball out of New Trier’s hands from then on.</p><p>Purcell scored on a nifty 12-yard run early in the fourth quarter to put Maine South ahead by two scores and nearly seal the win.</p><p>“That was a crucial third down,” Purcell said. “We called a pass and drew it up pretty well, but they covered it well. I just let my instincts take over, shed a tackle and got into the end zone. I’m just proud of my team and our linemen for blocking.” </p><p>Purcell was 12 of 14 passing for 180 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions. He had 14 carries for 88 yards and a score.</p><p>“We have a great team and something special,” Purcell said. “We proved it tonight. They had a lot of hype coming into this game. They deserved it. We knew it was going to be a battle.”</p><p>Ryder finished 19 of 37 passing for 216 yards with one touchdown and two interceptions. The first pick came on a jump ball at the end of the first half, when he was trying to make something happen. </p><p>Ryder had four carries for 14 yards and a touchdown. </p><p>“I’ve gotten to know [Ryder] a little bit,” Purcell said. “He’s a nice guy, and obviously he is getting some clout and recognition now. He deserves it. He was under-recruited, and he’s playing pretty well.
